9	The station stood at the very top of the Hollow where the road bends and then goes to nothing but the ridge. It was a low building, whitewashed, cold as a spring house inside even in August, and it smelled of milk and steam and hot iron, and you could hear the engine going before you came round the last turn. Ansel Keddie ran it. He went up there in ninety-five, the year before they opened it, to get it ready, and he tested that first summer too, and he was still there when I was a girl big enough to ride on the wagon with my father, so you can count that up and see how long a man can stand in one room.

He wrote in it standing up at a slope desk by the window where the light came in. If a man came in and asked him what his milk had done, he did not have to hunt. He turned to the day and he read it off. He tested a thousand cans a week and never a blot in that book, and I heard my father say more than once that if the rest of the world kept its accounts the way Ansel Keddie kept his there would be no lawyers in Ashlin. Which was my father's way of talking. There are still lawyers in Ashlin.

### Story 5: The Inspection and Condemnation (June 1923)

On June 12, 1923, Merle Strawn, the state dairy inspector for the Ordell circuit, visited the Ostrey Hollow station on his routine rounds. He had visited annually or biennially since 1907 and had never found added water. On this visit, carrying a new tool—a calibrated burette issued to field men starting in 1921—Strawn ran the station's milk pipettes against the burette to verify their delivery.

The glass would not deliver its mark. Strawn condemned the entire crate—all original pipettes from 1897—on the spot. He directed the manager to order new equipment immediately. His circuit book entry reads: "These measures will not deliver their mark. Condemned the lot, the whole crate of them, and told the manager to order new. Glass is glass and I did not weigh what it has cost them."

On June 28, 1923, the Association wrote to Ammon & Sons ordering replacement pipettes and bottles. Ammon's reply, July 2, 1923, confirmed the order would go forward that month but stated: "Our books of the nineties are not such that we can tell you anything about the lot you name." New glass was in use by July; the station's own broken measure was replaced the same summer.

Crucially, no one at the time connected the condemnation to the 26-year history of low tests. The condemned glass was carried to the loft above the intake room, placed in a wooden crate, covered with a tarpaulin, and left there. No one asked questions. Strawn made no inference about past tests. The Association saw it as routine maintenance—apparatus wears, must be replaced. No mention was made in the office records or minutes. ### C1. The proportion of error from the glassware

**(a) By what proportion did the station's tests differ from the truth?**

The pipettes were blown for 17.6 cc but delivered 16.72 cc (mean of nine surviving pipettes, per Ivy Keddie's measurement on March 9, 1958, r04).

Proportion: 16.72 ÷ 17.6 = 0.9244 (or 92.44 hundredths)

The tests read 92.44% of the true value, meaning they were short by 1 − 0.9244 = **0.0756 or 7.56 hundredths of the mark, or equivalently one part in twenty (1/20 = 0.05 = 5%).**

Ivy Keddie (r04) states: "Every test made at that station with that glass read ninety-five percent of the truth," rounding 0.9244 to 0.95. The exact figure from the nine pipettes is 16.72/17.6 = 0.9244.

**(b) True average and recorded shortfall:**

The recorded average for the affected years was 3.61 percent (per Ansel Keddie's 1922 summary leaf, r03, r04, r07, r22).

True average = 3.61 ÷ 0.9244 = 3.905 percent

Shortfall = 3.905 − 3.61 = **0.295 points (or approximately 0.30 points)**

**However**, Ivy Keddie rounds the calculation: "Three point six one divided by ninety-five hundredths is three point eight" (r04). Using 0.95 (her stated proportion): 3.61 ÷ 0.95 = 3.8. This gives a shortfall of 0.19 points, which matches the observed gap of 0.19 that patrons had been complaining of since 1902.

- Using 0.95: 3.61 ÷ 0.95 = 3.8, shortfall = 0.19
- Using 0.9244: 3.61 ÷ 0.9244 = 3.905, shortfall = 0.295
